title: Takashi Nagai
hook: a Catholic doctor in Nagasaki who kept treating the wounded after the bomb killed his wife

segments.voice: Yesterday, Edith Stein, and her whole story. Your line was for my people. Whose story did you listen to, all the way to the end? Day nine hundred fifty-six.

In the ashes of a kitchen, a man kneels and picks up a few blackened bones, and beside them, a melted chain of rosary beads. He knows whose they are. He is a doctor, a radiologist, and a few days earlier he was at work in his hospital in Nagasaki when the atomic bomb fell. Bleeding from his own wounds, he spent those days treating other people. Only then did he come home to look for his wife, Midori. He carries what he found back in a bucket. Today, Takashi Nagai, and the bell that rang again.

Nagai grew up outside the church and came to Catholic faith as a young man, in Nagasaki's Urakami district, where Christian families had kept their faith in secret through long years of persecution. His wife Midori came from one of those families. By the time the bomb fell, he was already ill. Years of work with X-rays, without much protection, had given him leukemia. The bomb made everything worse. He set up first aid in the ruins, with the staff who were still alive, and worked until he collapsed. His children survived because they had been sent to the countryside. Afterward he lived with them in a tiny hut near the ruins of the cathedral. He named it for a line of Jesus. In the King James Bible: "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." From his bed, as his illness grew, he wrote books, including one called The Bells of Nagasaki. The title comes from the cathedral. Its bells had been buried in the rubble, and when the people dug one out, it rang again, and to him it sounded like a promise that the city would live. Nagai also spoke of the bombing in religious terms, as a sacrifice, and other survivors and writers have strongly disagreed with that. It's fair to say his words comforted some and troubled others. What's harder to argue with is what he did with his hands. He grieved and he worked, both at once. Jesus said, in Matthew: "Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted." Nagai didn't wait to be comforted before he started caring for others.
screen: `A HUT NAMED FOR LOVE OF NEIGHBOR.`
`THE BELL DUG OUT OF THE RUBBLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: care while grieving. Settle, and breathe. If you're carrying a loss right now, a person, a place, a plan, let yourself name it. Don't hurry it away. Then notice who else is near you who might need something. A child. A friend. A coworker who looks tired. Nagai didn't wait until his grief was finished. Ask what one small act of care you could do today, not instead of grieving but alongside it. If you're not grieving now, bring to mind someone who is, and what might help them. If you pray, you can say the line from Matthew: blessed are they that mourn. The bell holds the time.
Takashi Nagai. A Catholic doctor in Nagasaki who lost his wife to the atomic bomb, kept treating the wounded, and wrote The Bells of Nagasaki.
Your line: the bells of nagasaki. Today, if you hear a bell, a chime or a phone alert, let it remind you of one person to care for, even on a heavy day. Day nine hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: In Nagasaki, Nagai's hut is preserved beside a memorial museum, and Catholics in the Urakami community remember the bombing each August with Mass and prayer for peace at the rebuilt cathedral.

notes: Claims rule: no dates (9 August 1945, his death 1951), no casualty figures, no count of his children or of days before he went home ('a few days' is used).
The hut, Nyokodo (如己堂, 'as-yourself hall'), is named for 'love thy neighbour as thyself'; the Japanese name is not given in the voice. Confirm.
Leukemia diagnosed before the bombing from radiology work: confirm.
'Carries what he found back in a bucket': widely told detail; confirm or cut.
His children survived because they had been sent to the countryside (to their grandmother): confirm.
The bell: the Angelus bell of Urakami Cathedral, dug out and rung again (Christmas 1945); confirm phrasing.
His 'burnt offering' (hansai) reading of the bombing is described without quotation and noted as contested; confirm it is fair to both sides.
Japanese 長崎の鐘 and the pronunciation guide: confirm.
howItsDone: confirm Nyokodo is beside the Nagai Takashi Memorial Museum.
